top3.why: Philly DSA's Socialist Night School turns to abolition this week, tracing the fight to defund police and prisons here back to global movements against racial capitalism and imperialism. It's political education in the true sense — an internationalist abolitionist framework, not just local talking points. Free, at Wooden Shoe, the city's anarchist bookstore and the most reliable venue in town for exactly this kind of programming.

Collector Edward Leahy opens up eight centuries of literary history for one intimate evening at the Rosenbach — illuminated manuscripts, jeweled bindings, incunabula, and what's likely the world's finest private Beatrix Potter collection, alongside first editions of horror classics. A rare chance to hear a serious collector talk through how and why he built this, not just look at it behind glass.

Mike Diamond — Mike D of the Beastie Boys — brings his “5D” tour to Union Transfer, a rare non-NYC stop from a founding figure of New York hip-hop who discovered punk rock as a teenager and never fully let go of it. Expect stories as much as a set: this reads as a conversational, career-spanning night rather than a straight concert. Spring Garden, a few blocks from the Broad Street Line's Spring Garden stop.

top3.why: Exhumed Films marks Bela Lugosi's 144th birthday with a 16mm double feature of White Zombie and Invisible Ghost at PhilaMOCA — the kind of print-hunting, genuinely obscure repertory booking this place exists for. $18.15, and a rare chance to see these on film instead of a stream.

A premiere screening with teeth: Philadelphia Film Society hosts the debut of “I Don't Want to Drink Your Blood Anymore,” part of this week's cluster of Halloween-season vampire programming around town. $18+, Center City.

Goth Shop & Social turns Tattooed Moms into a pop-up market for small goth-adjacent businesses, founded by a nonbinary trans goth of color — free, no cover, with Philly Punks With Lunches on hand for Narcan and safety resources. It's community infrastructure dressed as a market: the $1 raffle's proceeds go to local trans youth.

top3.why: Claudio Simonetti's Goblin perform their score live, synced to a screening of Dario Argento's Tenebre (1982) — then return after the film for a second set of other Goblin material, from a composer whose other scores (Suspiria, Dawn of the Dead, Deep Red, Demons) shaped horror cinema's sound as much as any director shaped its look. It's a trek: the Colonial Theatre is in Phoenixville, about 30 miles northwest of Center City, so plan on a car or a long transit day.

A new feature documentary on Rozz Williams — founder of deathrock pioneers Christian Death — gets its area premiere at PhilaMOCA, tracing the goth-punk lineage this venue's whole repertory program lives inside. Doors at 7, with the film following shortly after. $12.

A stacked no wave/noise-rock/post-punk bill — Subtle Body, Agita, Orchid Club (in from Minneapolis), and Crease — at Cousin Danny's, a DIY room keeping West Philly's underground alive. It's out past University City on Market Street; the Market-Frankford Line's 52nd Street stop is the closest way in without a car.

top3.why: L7 bring their “Last Hurrah” farewell tour to Brooklyn Bowl — a legitimately rare chance to see one of the loudest, funniest bands of the grunge/riot-grrrl crossover before they're off the road for good. All ages, general-admission standing room. It's out on the Fishtown/Olde Richmond waterfront with no direct rail line, so budget for a bus or a short rideshare from the Girard stop.

A one-person gothic horror performance about industrialization and masculinity in 19th-century Philadelphia, staged inside the genuinely haunted-feeling confines of Elfreth's Alley Museum — back for an extended run after selling out in 2025. $15, and about as site-specific as horror theater gets in this city.

PhilaMOCA hosts the Philly premiere of “Smoker's Lounge” plus a block of short films, with a cash prize for whoever shows up in the best handmade mask — real audience participation layered onto a real film premiere. Doors at 7, films start around 7:30; $15–20, less with a mask.

top3.why: Milwaukee's Old Pup brings a new experimental folk record built on pedal steel to Wooden Shoe, backed by Milk Dud and Michael Cormier-O'Leary — a quieter, stranger touring show than the bookstore's usual political programming, and a reminder its calendar isn't just talks and workshops. Suggested $10–15 donation, no one turned away for lack of funds.

Brittany Lynn and the Transducer Players bring back Philadelphia's longest-running Rocky Horror tradition — full shadow cast, full chaos, full audience participation. It's the kind of cult-horror-as-community-theater night that's been a Gayborhood fixture for years, not a one-off novelty booking.

Ars Nova Workshop — the city's most serious avant-garde jazz presenter — brings Cuban drummer Dafnis Prieto and his Sí o Sí Quartet to Solar Myth for a night of genuinely virtuosic, Afro-Cuban-rooted jazz. 21+, $43.26, South Broad.

top3.why: The Damned — one of the bands that invented UK punk in the first place — play Union Transfer on the kind of night Philly's punk and goth lineages both claim as their own. Decades in, they're still theatrical, still gothic, still genuinely dangerous live. Support from Flamin' Groovies and The Courettes rounds out a stacked bill.

George Hardy — the dentist-turned-accidental-icon of “Best Worst Movie” fame — returns to PhilaMOCA in person for a Halloween-season screening of TROLL 2, the gloriously inept 1990 cult object that's outlived every movie that was actually trying to be good. Expect a full post-screening Q&A, not just a film on a loop. $24.20.

Non-Compliant returns to Wooden Shoe for a night of queer disabled poets reading work under the title “Spells to Turn You Into a Transgender Communist” — leftist politics, disability justice, and literary performance in one room, exactly the overlap this bookstore exists to host. Free, South Street.

top3.why: Osees — the long-running, shape-shifting garage-punk project led by John Dwyer — bring their new record ABOMINATION REVEALED AT LAST. to Union Transfer, an album Dwyer describes as a direct, pummeling reaction to the current moment's stack of catastrophes. Loud, political, and uncompromising in exactly the way their decades-long catalog has trained you to expect.

Cory McAbee — the cult filmmaker behind THE AMERICAN ASTRONAUT — brings his musical feature THESE PEOPLE to PhilaMOCA in person. It's an assembled, genre-scrambling film about Lincoln's assassination, narrated by an immortal who was in the room, which is about as deep a cut as repertory programming gets here. $14.52.

Profs & Pints pairs an academic lecture with a bar crowd; this installment takes on the life of Frankenstein (the listing gives no further description beyond the title, so treat the specific angle as unconfirmed). It's in Fishtown; the Market-Frankford Line's Berks or Girard stop is the easiest way in without a car.
